name: Mukah Melanau
catalog_citation: Blust, Robert. 1988. Sketches of the morphology and phonology of Bornean languages 2: Mukah (Melanau). In H. Steinhauer (ed.), Papers in Western Austronesian Linguistics No. 3, 151-216. Pacific Linguistics A-78. Canberra: ANU.
catalog_locator: sec. 2.5.1 Phonological rules, rule 1 (stress placement), pp. 178-179
catalog_quote: 1 (stress placement) As stress placement in Mukah citation forms is apparently governed by a rather complex set of conditions, it will perhaps be clearest if the general case (a) is stated first, followed by each subcase (b-d) in descending order of importance: (a) the penultimate vowel of a word receives stress. ... (b) if the penultimate vowel of a word is schwa, stress shifts to the final syllable. ... (c) following /a/ and preceding word boundary high vowels receive stress (and perhaps added length - not mentioned further). This subpart of the stress rule is posited to account for the fact that minimal pairs such as ... differ not only in number of syllables, but also in placement of stress. The shift of stress in such cases may be motivated by a desire to avoid homophony, or may have been a product of unnatural emphasis for my sake. ... In a sequence of like vowels the first vowel …

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the Blust 1988 text we hold at sec. 2.5.1 rule 1, pp. 178-179, with matching examples. (2) The source is a first-hand phonology/morphology sketch by Blust in Pacific Linguistics -- the only phonological description of the Mukah dialect; Glottolog's only larger work (Clayre 1972) is on the Dalat dialect. Web search found no instrumental or later prosodic study of Melanau; the 2016 Malaysian phonology article on Mukah (downloaded) treats segments only. Blust 2013 (held) and Smith 2023 (downloaded) both restate penultimate stress with final stress after a schwa penult, consistent with the 'weight-hedged, full-vs-reduced-vowel, right edge' coding; the hedging in our record mirrors Blust's own ('apparently', 'may have been a product of unnatural emphasis for my sake') and is appropriate. (3) list of works to obtain is short: Clayre 1972 (open at Edinburgh ERA but unreachable

sources.quote: 'Identical patterns are found in other Western Indonesian languages in Borneo, including In Mukah Melanau where Blust (1988: 178) notes that stress occurs typically on the penultimate syllable in phrasal contexts but that stress occurs on the final syllable if the penultimate syllable has a schwa nucleus.' (secondary, cites our deciding source; note Blust actually says 'citation forms', not 'phrasal contexts')
sources.locator: offprint p. [14] (section on Western Indonesian stress shift)
sources.note: Recent comparative treatment that restates the Mukah Melanau rule (penultimate; final after schwa penult) from Blust 1988:178 and frames schwa as weightless -- supports the weight (full-vs-reduced-vowel) reading of our 'weight-hedged' coding; usable as a corroborating secondary citation.
